data.title: Myanmar genocide judgment may bolster Gaza case against Israel
data.description:
Key points:
  • ICJ finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
  • Judges say genocide can coexist with military aims
  • South Africa says ruling sets important precedent for state genocide

By Anthony Deutsch and Stephanie van den Berg

The International Court of Justice's landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya will strengthen South Africa's genocide case against Israel over the war in Gaza, legal experts said, establishing a precedent that genocidal intent can coexist with a military objective.

While the conflicts in Gaza and Myanmar are legally distinct, both cases before the World Court are based on allegations that states breached their obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

On Thursday, the court found that Myanmar had violated the convention on multiple grounds stemming from mistreatment of the Muslim Rohingya minority by the armed forces.

South Africa, which has brought a genocide case against Israel over its conduct in Gaza, welcomed the judgment. Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said it set an important precedent by establishing for the first time that a state had committed genocide. He said it was of "great significance" to the case against Israel, which is not expected to be argued until 2029.

Both Myanmar and Israel have defended the actions of their armed forces as legitimate responses to insurgencies. But a majority of nine judges on the 15-member bench found that around 10,000 killings, including of children, the razing of homes, widespread sexual violence and the forced exodus of more than 700,000 people in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The ruling also handed other major legal victories to Gambia, which brought the case seven years ago on behalf of Muslim-majority countries.

The judges found that Myanmar had failed in its obligation to prevent genocide and said it must facilitate the return of Rohingya refugees and pay unspecified reparations.

The court also adopted conclusions from UN fact-finding reports, including one stating that mass deaths and rapes showed genocidal intent.

IMPORTANT PRECEDENT

Israeli legal scholar Yuval Shany said the ruling could broaden the arguments available to South Africa in its case against Israel.

He said the court maintained a requirement that genocidal intent be the “only reasonable inference,” but expanded the contextual factors it can consider beyond a pattern of conduct, to include the scale and systematic nature of acts and the history of persecution.

The approach “gives South Africa more avenues to argue for genocide” in Gaza, Shany said.

Proving genocide is notoriously difficult because it requires establishing an "intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such."

Five criminal acts can constitute genocide: killing members of a group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, creating conditions calculated to destroy them, preventing births, or forcibly transferring children to ​other groups.

Lamola said South Africa would study the judgment carefully with a view to demonstrating, as the court had in the Rohingya case, that a state's actions, including ethnic cleansing, the killing of children, sexual violence and destruction of civilian infrastructure, can fall within the definition of genocide.

TARGETING OF CHILDREN, WOMEN

Another aspect of the ruling that could resonate in the Israel case was the court's emphasis on the systematic nature and scale of the crimes committed in Myanmar, said Marieke de Hoon, professor of international criminal law at the University of Amsterdam.

South Africa alleges that Israel's military operations created conditions intended to prevent births and disproportionately affected women and children in Gaza. In its filing to the ICJ, it said an estimated 70% of those killed were non-combatants. Israel rejects those allegations and says its operations have been conducted in accordance with international law.

"Arguments that a military intent or military objective would erase the idea that there could be a genocide intent are now rejected by the court," said De Hoon.

She said the judges found that some acts, including attacks on children and women and sexual violence, could not be explained by military objectives alone, leaving genocide as the only reasonable inference.

The Hague Initiative for International Cooperation (Thinc), a think tank funded by pro-Israeli groups, said the judgment would fundamentally alter how courts assess allegations of genocide by imposing a "lower threshold for proving genocidal intent, with serious consequences for Western militaries engaged in confronting terror," such as after Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

It is "not only a verdict in a particular case but a template," Thinc's director, Andrew Tucker, wrote in a reaction.

"Its propositions will be used in future cases: that genocidal intent may coexist with legitimate military objectives...that UN reports compiled without access can carry decisive weight; and that a state can breach the duty to prevent genocide without any finding that genocide occurred."

While the World Court judgment unequivocally found Myanmar responsible for genocide, proving the crime in court remains difficult, said Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the International Crisis Group.

"The ICJ has never before found that a state committed genocide. The legal bar is extremely high, but what this case shows is that it is surmountable,” he said.

data.title: IRDAI slaps ₹2 cr penalty on Star Health & Allied Insurance
data.description:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has imposed a ₹2 crore penalty on Star Health and Allied Insurance Company for declining some health insurance claims related to Covid-19 on untenable grounds.

In an inspection conducted earlier, the Authority further found that the insurer had made deductions which were not supported by the policy terms, and in many sampled cases, the amount was paid only after the Authority highlighted them,’’ the insurance regulator said in an order issued on Friday.

Policyholders were not informed of the specific policy conditions under which claims were repudiated or reduced, depriving them of an informed basis to challenge these decisions.

The Authority has imposed a total penalty of ₹2 crore under Section 102 of the Insurance Act, 1938, comprising ₹2 crore for violation of various regulations related to claims and the third party administration, among others.

The insurer has also been warned for not ensuring that discounts agreed with network hospitals are reflected in hospital bills and made known to policyholders and was directed to ensure that its claim settlement letters itemise all allowed, disallowed, non-payable and discount amounts and the reduction in Sum Insured.

It was further cautioned for collecting renewal premium more than 90 days in advance and for not providing Insurance Ombudsman details to complainants, IRDAI said.

data.title: Eurozone Wage Growth Accelerates, But Remains Modest — 2nd Update
data.description:
By Paul Hannon

Eurozone wage growth accelerated slightly in the three months through September, but remained modest despite the pickup in inflation triggered by the war between the U.S. and Iran.

The European Central Bank on Friday said wages negotiated by labor unions and similar groups were 2.57% higher in the third quarter than a year earlier, an increase in the annual rate of growth from 2.45% in the three months through June.

In a separate release, the European Commission said eurozone consumers became less downbeat about their prospects in November, likely reflecting renewed hopes for a resolution of the conflict, and a sustained decline in energy prices, following the U.S. midterm elections.

Since the start of the war, officials at the ECB have highlighted the outcome of wage negotiations as a key indicator as to whether the jump in energy prices triggered by the conflict is set to keep inflation above their 2% target.

But there are few signs as yet that workers are securing larger pay rises to cover increased energy bills.

"What we don't see at the moment is second-round effects, not yet," Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin said in an interview with CNBC on Thursday. "We need to be vigilant about what will happen and that's the reason we've increased rates in the past."

The ECB raised its key rate in September and June.

The eurozone's annual rate of inflation rose to 4% in October from 1.9% in February, the month in which the war began.

That pickup in the pace of price rises has weakened the spending power of eurozone households, and for the year as a whole the European Commission now estimates that wages adjusted for inflation will increase by just 0.4%, a sharp slowdown from 1.8% in 2025.

It expects real wages to rise at a similarly slow pace next year, with the commission forecasting that compensation per worker will rise at an unchanged pace of 3.5%.

Against that backdrop, eurozone consumers are gloomy about the outlook, although they were less pessimistic in November than in the previous month.

The commission said its measure of consumer sentiment rose to minus 16.9 from minus 17.9, still well below the levels recorded before the start of the war, but above the lows reached immediately after the conflict began.

Hopes for a peace deal were boosted by the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections, in which voters voiced their opposition to the war and particularly its impact on prices.

data.title: SVRA Stock Hits 52-Week Low After FDA Delays Decision On Lung Disease Drug Application
data.description:
Key points:
  • Molgramostim, proposed to be marketed as Molbreevi, is expected to treat autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.
  • The FDA decision was initially set for August but later extended to November 22.
  • The company reported cash equivalents and short-term investments of about $173 million, as of June 30.

Shares of Savara (SVRA) plunged 18% on Friday to their lowest level in just over a year, after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said it would not meet the November 22 deadline to decide on the company’s experimental lung disease treatment, Molgramostim.

The company said the FDA’s review remains ongoing, but did not provide a revised date for the decision. The delay does not mean that the FDA has issued a Complete Response Letter (CRL) or rejected the application.

SVRA shares are on track for their biggest single-day slump since May 2025.

FDA’s Second Extension For Molbreevi

Molgramostim, proposed to be marketed as Molbreevi, treats autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), a rare disease in which fatty, protein-rich material accumulates in the lungs, making breathing difficult. The inhaled treatment helps immune cells clear the accumulated material.

Savara’s Phase 3 Impala-2 trial met its primary endpoint, with data showing significant improvements in lung function after 24 weeks compared with placebo. The FDA granted priority review, with a decision initially set for August but later extended to November 22.

Molbreevi is Savara’s only clinical development program. The company reported cash equivalents and short-term investments of about $173 million, as of June 30.

Last week, H.C. Wainwright initiated coverage with a ‘Buy’ rating and $10 price target, citing Molbreevi’s potential to become the first FDA-approved treatment for the disease.

JPMorgan initiated coverage in October with an ‘Overweight’ rating and $12 target, citing the drug’s blockbuster potential. The firm added that Molbreevi could receive approvals in the U.K. and European Union in the fourth quarter (Q4) of 2026 and the first quarter (Q1) of 2027.

Retail Remains 'Extremely Bullish'

Despite the slump, retail sentiment surrounding SVRA on Stocktwits remained ‘extremely bullish’ over the past 24 hours, amid ‘extremely high’ message volumes.

The stock has declined more than 29% so far in 2026.
